title: Quantum Oscillations of $\mathrm{Sr}_2\mathrm{RuO}_4$ under c-Axis Uniaxial Stress
authors: Fabian Jerzembeck, Maximilian T. Pelly, Helge Rosner, Edgar Abarca Morales, Naoki Kikugawa, Dmitry A. Sokolov, Andrew P. Mackenzie, Andreas W. Rost, Elena Hassinger, Javier F. Landaeta
abstract: Uniaxial stress has now been widely used to study correlated electron materials. However, Fermi surface-resolved experimental data on the evolution of the electronic structure under piezoelectrically applied stress are sparse, with no reports of de Haas-van Alphen (dHvA) effects under uniaxial stress. Here we present dHvA measurements under $c$-axis uniaxial stress on the unconventional superconductor $\mathrm{Sr}_2\mathrm{RuO}_4$. This allows us to study the evolution of the electronic structure directly and to gain insight into the contradicting behavior of the predicted enhancement of the electronic density of states and the observed suppression of $T_\text{c}$. We are able to follow all Fermi surfaces for stress up to $-1.8$~GPa and find that the cross-sectional areas of the hole-like $α$ sheet increase and electron-like $β$ sheet decrease. At the same time, the area of the electron-like $γ$ sheet increases. Therefore, in contrast to in-plane uniaxial stress, charge transfer is the mechanism for approaching the electron-to-hole Lifshitz transition and the associated Van Hove singularity. Additionally, we find that the effective masses on all three Fermi sheets are slightly enhanced as the Lifshitz transition is approached. We compare the dHvA results with quantum oscillations in the magnetostriction and band structure calculations, and find good agreement. At a more general level, our findings show that quantum oscillation measurements under uniaxial stress, combined with band-structure calculations, offer a promising new route for studying quantum materials.
summary: This work uses dHvA measurements on Sr2RuO4 under uniaxial stress to map out the evolution of its electronic structure. By observing changes in Fermi surface areas and effective masses, the authors propose that charge transfer is the key mechanism driving the system toward a Lifshitz transition. The findings establish quantum oscillation measurements as a powerful tool for probing correlated materials under external strain.
main_problem: To study how applying uniaxial stress affects the electronic structure and Fermi surface of the unconventional superconductor Sr2RuO4, particularly to reconcile discrepancies between predicted density of states changes and observed superconducting temperature suppression.
main_result: The application of c-axis uniaxial stress causes measurable changes in the cross-sectional areas of different Fermi sheets ($\alpha$ increases, $ eta$ decreases, $\gamma$ increases), suggesting charge transfer is driving the system toward a Lifshitz transition. Effective masses on all measured sheets are found to be slightly enhanced upon compression.
method: The study combines experimental De Haas-van Alphen (dHvA) quantum oscillation measurements under uniaxial stress with theoretical Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations and magnetostriction measurements for comparison.
model_or_system: The system is the unconventional superconductor Sr2RuO4. The analysis focuses on how applying controlled c-axis uniaxial strain/stress ($\sigma_{zz}$) tunes the electronic band structure, leading to changes in Fermi surface topology and carrier distribution among different orbital character sheets ($\alpha,  eta, \gamma$).
key_observables: dHvA frequencies (for $\alpha,  eta, \gamma$ sheets), cross-sectional areas of Fermi sheets, effective masses ($m^*$), superconducting critical temperature $T_c(\sigma)$, and strain/stress dependence ($\Delta F$ vs. $\sigma$).
important_parameters: Uniaxial stress up to $-1.8$ GPa (experimentally) or higher (theoretically); the approach to a Lifshitz transition; effective mass enhancement factor ($\sim 10\%$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that relative changes in effective masses are intrinsic and can be compared across different stress states, and that strain inhomogeneity issues can be controlled.
figures_summary: Figures show raw/normalized quantum oscillations vs. magnetic field under various stresses; comparisons between dHvA frequency shifts ($\Delta F$) derived from experiment and DFT calculations; and plots detailing the evolution of Fermi surface areas and $T_c$ dependence on stress.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the experimental feasibility of measuring dHvA effects under uniaxial stress. It then details how the measured changes in Fermi surface topology (sheet area changes) point to charge transfer mechanisms approaching a Van Hove singularity, contrasting this with other stress directions. Finally, it confirms quantitative agreement between these quantum oscillation results and DFT predictions.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter physics, the precise measurement of electronic structure evolution under external fields (stress) provides an excellent model for studying how external perturbations tune many-body ground states, which has parallels in controlling quantum phases relevant to AMO systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Schematic 2D Fermi surface of Sr2RuO4 under uniaxial stress. (a) Zero stress. (b) In-plane uniaxial stress |σxx| > |σcrit,xx|. (c) Out-of-plane uniaxial stress |σzz| > |σcrit,zz|.

Figure 2. (a) Raw dHvA oscillations as a function of magnetic field at 90 mK (stress cell temperature) for a series of compressive stresses. (b) Same data as in (a) plotted versus inverse field; curves are vertically shifted for clarity. (c–e) Fourier spectra highlighting the α, β, γ, and 2α +β peaks under different stresses. FFTs were taken over the field range 3–15 T for α and 8–15 T for the other Fermi surface sheets.

Figure 4. Comparison of the FFTs (8–15 T range) of quantum oscil- lations from magnetostriction (85 mK) and dHvA (125 mK) on the same sample. Before comparison, the strain FFT was multiplied by F2 (details are in the main text). Both spectra are then normalized to the α peak height. The inset shows the raw dilatometer signal (strain oscillations) as a function of field.

Figure 3. Lifshitz-Kosevich effective mass analysis at 0 GPa (circles, solid lines) and −1 GPa (squares, dashed lines). Uncertainties on the effective masses from the fits are estimated to be about 2% for the α and β sheets, and about 5% for the γ sheet.
